lessons.title: Subject and verb
lessons.tip: A sentence needs a subject (who or what) and a verb (the action or state). Put the subject first: “Maria runs.” “The dog sleeps.” Begin with a capital letter and end with a period.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)

activities.prompt: Which one is a complete sentence?
Pick the verb: “Tom reads every day.”
Match each verb with its meaning.
activities.answer: run = move fast on foot; sleep = rest at night; eat = take in food

activities.prompt: Find the mistake, then write the sentence correctly. Play children in the park.
True or false: A sentence needs a subject and a verb.
Your turn. Write three short sentences about your day. Each needs a subject and a verb.

lessons.title: Add an object
lessons.tip: Many sentences add an object, the person or thing that receives the action: “Sam eats an apple.” Keep the order subject, verb, object. English does not move the object to the front.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)

activities.prompt: Pick the object: “Sam eats an apple.”
Which sentence has the right order?
Type the object: “We open the window.”
Match each verb with the thing that goes with it.
activities.answer: drink = water; read = a book; kick = a ball

activities.prompt: Find the mistake, then write the sentence correctly. Open I the door.
Which sentence has a subject, a verb and an object?
True or false: In “Sam eats an apple,” the object is Sam.
Your turn. Write two sentences about what you eat or drink. Use a subject, a verb and an object.

lessons.title: Commands and requests
lessons.tip: A command starts with the verb: “Open the door.” Add “please” to be polite: “Please open the door.” To say what not to do, start with “Don't”: “Don't run.”
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)

activities.prompt: Which sentence tells someone NOT to do something?
Type the missing word: ___ be late.
Match each situation with a fitting command.
activities.answer: Someone is at the door. = Come in, please.; The baby is asleep. = Be quiet, please.; Your friend is lost. = Follow me.

activities.prompt: Find the mistake, then write the sentence correctly. Please you sit down.
True or false: A command usually starts with the verb.
Which word makes a command polite?
Your turn. Write three commands for a visitor to your home. Use “please” in one.

lessons.title: Join with and, but, or
lessons.tip: Join ideas with a small word. Use “and” to add, “but” to show a difference, and “or” to give a choice: “I like tea and coffee.” “I like tea, but I don't like coffee.” “Do you want tea or coffee?”
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)

activities.prompt: You want to add two things: I have a pen ___ a notebook.
You want to show a difference: I am small, ___ my brother is tall.
You offer a choice: Would you like tea ___ coffee?

activities.answer: She is tired, but she is happy.

accepted: She is tired, but she is happy.

activities.prompt: Type the missing word: Do you want rice ___ noodles?
Match each small word with its job.
activities.answer: and = adds an idea; but = shows a difference; or = gives a choice
Tom has a dog and a cat.

options: Tom has a dog and a cat.
Tom has a dog a cat and.
Tom and has a dog a cat.
Tom has and a dog cat.
accepted: Tom has a dog and a cat.

activities.prompt: True or false: We use “or” to give a choice.
Your turn. Write three sentences about yourself. Use and, but and or once each.

lessons.title: Am, is, are
lessons.tip: Use “am” with I, “is” with he, she and it, and “are” with you, we and they: “I am ready.” “She is ready.” “They are ready.”
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)

activities.prompt: Type the missing word: You ___ my friend.
Type the missing word: My name ___ Ana.
Match each pronoun with the form of be.
activities.answer: I = am; she = is; we = are

activities.prompt: Find the mistake, then write the sentence correctly. They is happy.
Your turn. Write four sentences about you and your family. Use am, is and are.

lessons.title: Have and has
lessons.tip: Use “has” with he, she, it and with one person or thing: “She has a bike.” Use “have” with I, you, we and they: “We have a car.”
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)

activities.prompt: Type the missing word: Tom ___ a bike.
Type the missing word: You ___ my book.
Match each thing with what it has.
activities.answer: A bike = has two wheels; A hand = has five fingers; A week = has seven days

activities.prompt: Find the mistake, then write the sentence correctly. She have a blue pen.
True or false: We say “He have a car.”
Your turn. Write four sentences about what you and your family have. Use have and has.

lessons.title: Do and does in questions
lessons.tip: To ask a yes/no question, start with “Do” or “Does.” Use “Does” with he, she and it: “Does she like tea?” Use “Do” with I, you, we and they: “Do you like tea?” After Do or Does, the main verb stays simple: like, not likes.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)

activities.prompt: Type the missing word: ___ your brother play football?
Match each question with a short answer.
activities.answer: Do you like tea? = Yes, I do.; Does she swim? = No, she doesn't.; Do they know you? = Yes, they do.

activities.prompt: Find the mistake, then write the sentence correctly. Does he plays the guitar?
True or false: We say “Does she likes music?”
Your turn. Write four questions for a new friend. Start two with Do and two with Does.

lessons.title: Don't and doesn't
lessons.tip: To say no, use “do not” (don't) or “does not” (doesn't) before the simple verb: “I don't like rain.” “He doesn't like rain.” Use doesn't with he, she and it.
sources: British Council-EAQUALS Core Inventory for General English (topic order and level)

activities.prompt: Type the missing word: The shop ___ open on Sunday.
Match each sentence with its negative.
activities.answer: I like tea. = I don't like tea.; She likes tea. = She doesn't like tea.; They like tea. = They don't like tea.

activities.prompt: Find the mistake, then write the sentence correctly. She don't like milk.
True or false: We say “He doesn't likes it.”
Your turn. Write four things you don't do on Sunday. Then write one thing your friend doesn't do.
